title: How Zero Population Growth Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore zero population growth and overpopulation debates. They cover Thomas Malthus and carrying capacity, Paul Ehrlich's 1968 book The Population Bomb and his alarmist predictions, fertility and replacement rates, the wanted vs. unwanted fertility gap, the work of Population Connection (formerly Zero Population Growth), critics who call overpopulation a myth and stress human ingenuity, economic arguments about aging populations and birth rates, consumption and environmental impact, and John B. Calhoun's 1970s rat and mouse "Universe 25" experiments on the "behavioral sink." The episode ends with listener mail about linguistic descriptivism and a request about speedwriting shorthand.

segments.title: Opening banter and previous episodes
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about the weather and gin and tonic season, then point listeners to earlier episodes on Thomas Malthus, Norman Borlaug and population.

segments.title: Paul Ehrlich and The Population Bomb
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Stanford biologist Paul Ehrlich, his 1968 book The Population Bomb with its dire predictions of famine in the 1970s, and the Malthusian roots of his argument. They also discuss the Zero Population Growth group he co-founded.

segments.title: Fertility rates and replacement rate
segments.summary: The hosts explain how fertility rate is calculated, global birth rates in the 1960s, and the replacement rate of about 2.1 births per woman in developed countries, higher in developing ones, with the extra 0.07 from male-biased births.

segments.title: Population growth, life expectancy and infant mortality
segments.summary: The hosts note that world population grew from about 1.6 billion to 7.2 billion over 110 years, driven by longer lifespans and lower infant mortality, and discuss how age structure affects the working-age population.

segments.title: Hunger, slums and resource use
segments.summary: The hosts cite statistics on hunger and malnutrition, clean water access, and urban slums, and discuss how American consumption and beef's water footprint factor into carrying capacity debates.

segments.title: Unmet need for contraception and the education hurdle
segments.summary: Population Connection's goal of giving women access to contraception is discussed, along with the finding that few women cite lack of access as the reason for unwanted pregnancies, with family and social pressure and misunderstanding of conception being more common reasons.

segments.title: Critics, human ingenuity and economic arguments
segments.summary: Critics say overpopulation is a myth, that Ehrlich's predictions failed, and that human ingenuity will solve problems. The hosts discuss the economic argument that low birth rates strain economies, and that education and contraception rights lower birth rates. They note that carbon emissions track per capita income more than population growth.

segments.title: Population Connection FAQ and the Texas argument
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the Population Connection FAQ and discuss the claim that the world's population could fit in Texas, which they say misses the point about carrying capacity.

segments.title: John Calhoun's Universe 25 and the behavioral sink
segments.summary: The hosts describe John B. Calhoun's mouse utopia experiments, especially Universe 25 begun in 1970 with eight mice that grew until social breakdown and extinction. They cover the behavioral sink concept, his 1962 Scientific American paper, cultural echoes in literature and film such as ZPG, Soylent Green and The Rats of NIMH, and Calhoun's more optimistic view of high-social-velocity mice and space colonization ideas.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close with a reminder to search for more information and a list of ways to contact the show.
